newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy within reach of key Maastricht goal - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Italy within reach of key Maastricht goal - OECD.

text.p: Italy might succeed in cutting its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, helping it to qualify for European economic and monetary union, the OECD said in a report released on Wednesday.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said despite a weaker than expected economy, government budget plans might enable Italy to comply with tough criteria for countries wishing to join the planned single European currency.

"While real GDP is projected to increase less rapidly than officially expected, announced fiscal measures, together with the related trend towards interest-rate convergence, have brought the Maastricht deficit objective within reach in 1997," the Paris-based OECD said in its year-end economic outlook.

Under the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, founder states of the new single currency, which is due to be launched in 1999, must have a deficit/GDP ratio of three percent. A decision on which countries qualify will be made early in 1998.

The OECD's year-end Economic Outlook, reviewing growth in its 27 member countries, is due to be published on December 19 but the Organisation allowed the early release of the report on Italy after an Italian domestic news agency broke the embargo.

The OECD forecast that the Italian economy would grow by 1.2 percent next year and 2.1 percent in 1998 against a government target of two percent and 2.8 percent respectively. It saw GDP growth of 0.8 percent in 1996, as does the government.
It said exports would lead the pick-up, helping Italy's already healthy trade surplus to widen further.
"Along with large net receipts from tourism, this should sustain a current account surplus of around four percent of GDP in 1997-98," the OECD report said.

It predicted that Italy's deficit/GDP ratio would be 3.7 percent in 1997, but added that this forecast did not take into account a 12.5 trillion lire ($8.2 billion) deficit reducing package included in the government's 1997 austerity budget.
Details of the package, which were released last month were not ready when the OECD completed its report, the Organisation said.
The Italian Treasury says the 12.5 trillion lire of measures represent 0.7 percent of GDP.
The budget, which aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire from next year's projected deficit, is expected to be ratified by parliament before the end of December.
The OECD predicted that this year's public sector deficit would settle at around 124 trillion lire. Latest forecasts within Italy point to a deficit of around 140 trillion lire.
Although some of the 1997 budget plans were just one-off items, Italy's deficit/GDP ratio was set to fall further in 1998 because of cyclical revenue gains and lower interest rates, the OECD said.
The differential between 10-year Italian and German government bonds have plummeted this year, touching 173 basis points on Wednesday against 490 points at the end of last year.

"Given fiscal consolidation and disinflation, interest rates are projected to continue to decline, with the long term differential vis-a-vis Germany coming down below one percentage point by the end of 1998," the OECD said.

At the start of 1996, inflation stood at 5.8 percent year-on-year. It has fallen sharply in recent months, touching 2.6 percent in November and the OECD said a government goal to get inflation down to two percent in 1998 may be possible.
But despite an improved macro-economic picture, the OECD warned that the unemployment rate would remain stuck at around 12 percent until the end of 1998. $1 = 1,524 lire
